text:
An autoencoder is a neural network architecture designed to learn efficient data representations by encoding input data into a lower-dimensional latent space and then decoding it back to the original space. It consists of two primary components: an encoder function that maps messages to a code (latent representation), and a decoder function that reconstructs the message from the code. The training process involves minimizing a loss function, typically based on reconstruction error (such as L2 loss), to optimize the parameters of the encoder and decoder so that the output closely resembles the input. To prevent the model from simply copying the input, the code space is often made smaller than the input space, creating an "undercomplete" autoencoder that performs dimensionality reduction. Variations include the Variational Autoencoder (VAE), which models the latent space as a probability distribution to enable generative sampling, and the Denoising Autoencoder (DAE), which learns robust representations by training on corrupted inputs.
The text also describes related architectures that utilize autoencoder principles. Sparse Autoencoders enforce sparsity in the latent code to improve interpretability and classification performance. Contractive Autoencoders add regularization to make the encoding process less sensitive to small input perturbations. Additionally, Bidirectional GANs (BiGAN) and Adversarial Autoencoders (AAE) integrate autoencoder structures with adversarial training to improve feature learning and discriminative capabilities. Modern implementations, such as those using Vision Transformers (ViT) or Masked Autoencoders (MAE), apply these concepts to computer vision tasks like image reconstruction and self-supervised pretraining.
